text: Mean text recovery over the 1,000-file corpus is 90.67%.
quote: Experimental results show an average text recovery rate of 90.67 %

text: Tail truncation (C10): Save As 99.57% vs Print to PDF 35.35%.
quote: ‘Save As’ averaged 99.57 %, whereas ‘Print to PDF’ averaged 35.35 %

text: Authors hypothesize (untested) that Print-to-PDF places text streams and font resources near EOF, explaining the C10 gap.
quote: We hypothesize that this gap arises from layout differences: ‘Print to PDF’ tends to place text streams and font resources near the end of the file.

text: Zlib tampering (C9) leaves unrecoverable segments depending on where the byte was changed; recovery ~60%.
quote: which creates unrecoverable segments depending on the location of the corruption

text: C4 loses up to 2% when /Pages and /Page are adjacent: the deleted span also removes the neighbouring page's font/image mappings.
quote: We observed a small reduction in recovery rate (≤ 2 %) from those files where a /Pages object and a /Page object were stored adjacent to each other.

text: Single-component synthetic damage: unclear how often such patterns occur in the wild.
quote: the assumption of damage to a single component makes it unclear how frequently such damage patterns occur in real-world environments

text: Use real-world corrupted files, or datasets reflecting realistic damage patterns derived from them.
quote: Using corrupted PDF files collected from real-world cases as datasets, or constructing datasets that reflect realistic damage patterns derived from analysis of such files

text: All corpus PDFs were produced by Microsoft Word only.
quote: the PDF files used in this study were generated using only Microsoft Word

text: Evaluate on PDFs from other producers and scanned-document conversions.
quote: Evaluating the proposed framework on PDF files produced through such diverse methods would help validate its broader applicability

text: Font repair fails when the damaged font is not in the pre-built font database.
quote: our approach is limited when the damaged font file does not exist in the pre-built font database

text: A more systematic, extensible font database across languages and fonts is an open challenge.
quote: constructing a more systematic and extensible font database to broaden recovery coverage across diverse languages and fonts remains an important challenge

text: Dictionary-based font mapping struggles for Arabic (word forms change with grammatical context); Arabic C6 ~33-40%.
quote: dictionary-based font mapping becomes challenging in languages like Arabic, where word forms change depending on the grammatical context

text: Replace the interactive font-choice step with AI-based contextual understanding.
quote: if this step can be replaced with AI-based contextual understanding

text: Conclusion: expand the font DB and incorporate AI to raise recovery and cut processing time.
quote: Future work will focus on expanding the font database and incorporating methods such as AI

text: Images whose placement is lost are only extracted to separate files, not re-placed on pages.
quote: For images, because precise placement is not possible, we extract the image data and store it as a separate file.

text: Ground truth is OCR (Google Document AI) of the original PDFs; exact word matches counted.
quote: the OCR results of the original PDF files were used as ground truth

text: Baselines were three end-user tools (iLovePDF Desktop, Repairit, PDF24 Creator); no open-source repair engines.
quote: including iLovePDF Desktop (iLovePDF, 2025), Repairit (Wondershare, 2025), and PDF24 Creator

text: Implementation uses pikepdf (qpdf bindings) and fontTools in Python.
quote: pikepdf (v9.5.1) is employed to create and manipulate objects in the template PDF files

text: Threat model = accidental damage: file-system loss, transmission encode/decode errors, interrupted downloads.
quote: Common causes include partial data loss on file systems, encoding or decoding errors during transmission, and interrupted or incomplete downloads.

text: Repair relies on a pre-constructed external font database inserted into the output (synthesized, not recovered, content).
quote: utilizes a preconstructed font database to ensure text within each page is interpreted correctly

text: Evaluation rendering used a single viewer (Chrome's built-in PDF viewer).
quote: the built-in viewer in the Google Chrome Web Browser was used for all assessments

text: Our reading: Table 2 per-language means do not reproduce Table 5 aggregates (e.g., C6 Save As 85.63 vs 88.12); C7/C8 Save As rows identical; two commercial baselines report identical C6-C8 numbers. Treat REPDF's per-class numbers as approximate until replicated.

Our reading: no fragmentation, mid-file holes, head truncation, compound faults, ObjStm/xref-stream damage, incremental-update or encrypted/signed files are evaluated; C2 removes a classic xref table only.

Our reading: OCR word-match rewards visually correct output even when text is not extractable/searchable, adds OCR error, ignores reading order, layout fidelity and non-text structure (annotations, outlines, forms, structure tree), and reports no runtimes or per-file distributions.

Our reading: font inference decodes via reverse cmap assuming gid stability; GSUB-produced glyphs (Arabic positional forms, Indic conjuncts, ligatures) never appear in cmap, which may explain Arabic failures better than the paper's 'inflection' account. Type1 (/FontFile), CFF (/FontFile3) and Type3 fonts are not handled.
